title: 'US Is Shooting Itself in the Foot': Experts Warn H-1B Crackdown Risks Innovation Drain
excerpt: Policy analysts and business leaders say the cumulative weight of H-1B restrictions is pushing talent overseas and accelerating the shift of high-value work to India's Global Capability Centers.
body:
• Immigration policy experts and business groups warn Trump's H-1B restrictions are pushing skilled workers and high-value jobs to competitor nations.
  • US technology firms are accelerating work shifts to India, where 1,700 Global Capability Centers now handle AI development, drug discovery, and cybersecurity.
  • The Cato Institute warns proposed fee structures "will crush the H-1B program," while the US Chamber of Commerce says costs are becoming "cost-prohibitive" for startups.
  • Universities and hospitals that depend on H-1B talent say restrictions threaten research and could worsen a projected shortage of 86,000 doctors.

A Growing Chorus of Concern

As the Trump administration stacks new restrictions on the H-1B visa program — from six-figure fees to tighter wage requirements and increased workplace investigations — a growing number of economists, policy analysts, and business leaders are warning that the United States is undermining its own competitive position in the global talent market.

“This is an arbitrary restriction that represents the US kind of shooting itself in the foot,” said Connor O’Brien, a high-skilled immigration fellow at the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based research organization, referring to restrictions on H-1B hiring at research institutions.

The criticism comes amid a cascade of policy changes that have reshaped the H-1B landscape in 2026: a $100,000 entry fee now blocked by a federal court, a proposed $103,265 application fee, higher prevailing-wage requirements, expanded workplace investigations by the Labor Department, and efforts to eliminate the 60-day grace period for laid-off workers.

Tech Firms Shift Work Overseas

Rather than absorb the mounting costs and regulatory uncertainty, major US technology firms are accelerating their shift of high-value work to India, according to Reuters. India hosts 1,700 Global Capability Centers — more than half the worldwide total — which have evolved from back-office support hubs into centers of AI development, cybersecurity research, drug discovery, and financial engineering.

“GCCs are uniquely positioned for this moment. They serve as a ready in-house engine. Plans are already underway.”

— Rohan Lobo, Partner and GCC Industry Leader, Deloitte India

“There is a sense of urgency,” said Lalit Ahuja, founder and CEO of ANSR, which helped FedEx, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Target, and Lowe’s set up GCCs in India. If visa restrictions continue unchallenged, industry experts say US firms could move their most strategic functions — product development, AI research, advanced analytics — to Indian operations rather than fight to bring workers to the United States.

Universities and Hospitals Sound the Alarm

The impact extends well beyond Silicon Valley. American universities and hospitals, which depend heavily on H-1B workers for research and clinical positions, have emerged as vocal opponents of the fee increases.

The University of Michigan, which employs roughly 850 H-1B workers, estimated that the $100,000 fee alone would cost the institution $9 million annually, according to court filings. Its administrators described the fee as “effectively a new tax on bringing some of the best minds to America.”

In healthcare, advocates point to a projected shortage of 86,000 doctors over the next decade. Some 23,000 foreign-trained physicians used H-1B visas between 2001 and 2024, making the program a critical pipeline for medical talent. St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, the Cleveland Clinic, and Massachusetts General Hospital collectively employ nearly 500 H-1B workers.

The Economic Stakes

David Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, argued the combined fee proposals would be devastating to both the H-1B program and the broader economy.

“The new fee-tax will crush the H-1B program, resulting in the loss of hundreds of thousands of talented workers,” Bier wrote. “The H-1B fee will undermine American innovation, competitiveness, fiscal security, and ultimately prosperity.”

Neil Bradley, chief policy officer at the US Chamber of Commerce, which is fighting the fee in federal court, warned that the higher costs “will make it cost-prohibitive for even more US employers — especially the thousands of start-ups and small and midsize businesses who rely on H-1Bs — to utilize the program.”

The Chamber’s position is notable given the traditional alignment of business groups with Republican administrations, highlighting the unusual politics of the H-1B debate within Trump’s own coalition.

A Global Competition for Talent

As the United States tightens its doors, other nations are moving in the opposite direction. China has promoted its “K visa” as an alternative to the H-1B. The United Kingdom is considering reducing visa fees for STEM workers. Germany’s ambassador to India publicly invited Indian professionals to consider opportunities there. South Korea and Japan have signaled similar plans.

Data from the past year offers a stark illustration: during the five months Trump’s $100,000 fee was in effect, only 85 new H-1B applications were filed from abroad — an 87% drop from historical norms. The government collected $28 million less than it would have under the previous structure.

For India’s professional community in the United States, the cumulative effect of these restrictions adds new urgency to decisions about career planning, family stability, and whether the American dream remains worth the wait. With proposed fees, tighter enforcement, and a 179-year green card backlog, the calculus is shifting in ways that may prove difficult to reverse.
